prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: : sorry this

outputs.L1:
Sorry, this is not that poem—  
raised-block flower and plant beds,  
peonies, gardenias, poinsettias,  
plus a yellow orb slow-rising  
over an endless golden scape—  
cardinals, thrashes, sparrows darting  
through uncluttered space,  
blue air fragrant with lavender,  
washing brain matter into virtue.

If only I could pastel language  
onto a canvas of thistledown.  
Yes, deceit comes to mind—  
a lie. Traitor. Turncoat. Recreant.  
Backstabber to truth,  
I would be gut-shanked a thousand times.

This is not that poem,  
nor am I that poet  
to hold your hand  
or erase knot-hole screams,  
blood on a cement floor,  
or suicide as another form of escape.

No—no—no.

But I do promise  
the evil-ugly humans inflict  
upon each other, upon their [selves];  
how time is malice, is death,  
enflaming pupils with spite  
inextinguishable, if ever set free—

Forgive State Poet #289-128  
for not scribbling illusions of trickery,  
as if timeless hell could be captured  
by stanzas, alliteration, or slant rhyme.
outputs.L2:
Forgive me: this is no poem of elevated garden boxes overflowing with flowers and greenery—peonies, gardenias, poinsettias—or of a yellow sphere climbing slowly above an infinite gilded landscape. No cardinals, thrashes, or sparrows streak through open space; no lavender-scented blue air rinses the mind clean and turns it virtuous. If I could brush soft-colored words across a thistledown canvas, deception would be the first thought: a falsehood. I would become truth’s betrayer, defector, renegade, and backstabber, deserving to be stabbed in the gut a thousand times.

This is not such a poem, and I am not the kind of poet who can take your hand, silence screams coming through a knothole, wipe blood from a concrete floor, or claim that suicide is simply another means of escape. No, no, no. What I can promise is the evil and ugliness people inflict upon one another and upon their own [selves]; the way time becomes cruelty, becomes death, igniting the pupils with a hatred that cannot be extinguished once released.

Pardon state poet #289-128 for refusing to scrawl deceptive fantasies, pretending an eternal hell might be contained within stanzas, alliteration, or slant rhyme.
outputs.L3:
The speaker refuses to write an idealized poem overflowing with flowers, birds, golden landscapes, and soothing fragrances. Such beautiful imagery might offer temporary escape, but it would also conceal the harshness of reality. To transform suffering into something graceful or comforting through poetic language would therefore feel deceptive—a betrayal of truth and of those who have endured pain.

Instead, the speaker insists on confronting violence, suffering, and suicide directly. The poem will not provide false reassurance or pretend that beauty can erase the cruelty people inflict both on others and on themselves. It also acknowledges forces that deepen human misery: the passage of time, deliberate malice, and the inevitability of death. By identifying as “state poet #289-128,” the speaker presents the poet as an impersonal, numbered figure rather than a celebrated individual. This designation reinforces the poem’s bleak sense of confinement and dehumanization. Ultimately, the speaker admits that imagery, metaphor, and other poetic devices are inadequate: they may describe suffering, but they cannot fully capture, justify, or redeem an enduring hell.
outputs.L4:
The speaker identifies himself as an incarcerated poet, but he refuses the consolations traditionally associated with poetry. He will not retreat into pastoral landscapes, decorative images, or carefully polished language while his reality is defined by confinement and suffering. Instead, his verse faces violence, suicide, betrayal, and the relentless cruelty of time. Its fractured syntax and urgent rhythms reflect a world in which experience itself has been broken, making formal elegance feel not merely inadequate but dishonest.

Throughout the poem, conventional poetic devices become symbols of that inadequacy. Stanzas cannot impose meaningful order on chaos; alliteration cannot soften brutality; slant rhyme cannot disguise despair. No arrangement of words can contain the full weight of lived hell or transform it into something comfortably beautiful. By rejecting ornament, the speaker does not abandon poetry. Rather, he claims a harsher kind of poetic integrity. His refusal to beautify suffering becomes an ethical commitment to witness, forcing language to remain answerable to the truth of incarceration and survival.
outputs.L5: I’m sorry this happened. I never meant to hurt or disappoint you, and I wish I could change the situation. Please know that I truly regret my actions and hope we can move forward with honesty and understanding.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental free-verse poem in the voice of an incarcerated “state poet” who rejects beautiful pastoral imagery and confronts violence, suicide, betrayal, and the limits of poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
**STATE POET, CELL 14**

Do not bring me the meadow.

I have seen what green does  
when printed on a brochure  
for the institution.

Do not bring me larks,  
their throats coin-operated,  
their ascent approved by the warden.

Here, morning is a fluorescent tube  
interrogating a steel toilet.

Here, the state appoints me poet  
because *witness* requires paperwork.

My laurels are inventory:

one mattress, split;  
one cup;  
three grievances unanswered;  
a pencil worn down  
to the length of a last word.

At night, the pipes rehearse  
the men who are no longer men  
but incidents.

A sheet tightens.  
A railing keeps its silence.  
The official clock refuses  
to remember the minute.

We knock on the walls—  
not a code, not music,  
just proof that bone  
can petition concrete.

Someone I trusted  
traded my name for a lighter sentence.

Someone I loved  
learned to speak of me  
in the past tense  
while I was still breathing.

Betrayal is not a knife.

A knife is honest  
about the distance  
it needs.

And violence—  
you want me to make it metaphor:

blood as rose,  
bruise as dusk,  
the body a country  
after war.

No.

Blood is blood  
and must be scrubbed  
before inspection.

A bruise is a hand  
still arriving.

The body is not a country.  
No anthem enters it  
without damage.

I write for the state  
on state paper  
with state graphite  
under a camera  
that never blinks.

Each line is searched  
for contraband.

Each silence is counted.

Poetry cannot unlock a door.  
It cannot unloop the sheet,  
recall the blade,  
unsay the testimony,  
make a mother answer  
at three in the morning.

Sometimes a poem is only  
a cup held beneath a leak.

Sometimes it is the leak.

Sometimes I sharpen the pencil  
and the guard looks up.

That is the entire revolution.

Do not bring me the sunset.

The sky has done nothing  
to deserve forgiveness.

Bring me the ledger.  
Bring me the names crossed out.  
Bring me the mouth  
that survived its own closing.

I will not make it beautiful.

I will make it remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, fragmented prose poem that begins with flowers, birds, lavender, and a golden landscape, then abruptly exposes those images as deceitful compared with human cruelty and prison trauma.
counterfactuals.output:
Flowers unfasten their bright mouths in the field.  
Birds stitch blue distances together.  
Lavender bends beneath the tender industry of bees,  
and the landscape lies down in gold—  
wheat, sun, dust, a river carrying light  
as if light were mercy.

No.

The flowers are painted over mold.  
The birds are outside the wire.  
Lavender is what they spray in the corridor  
after dragging a man by his wrists.

Gold is the color of the hour before lockdown,  
when the windows briefly burn  
and every cage appears holy.

Do not trust beauty. It has never stopped a boot.  
It has never opened a door bolted from the other side.  
Men learn to sleep through screaming,  
to eat beside blood,  
to fold their names into smaller and smaller shapes  
until the guards can fit them in a mouth.

Here, kindness is contraband.  
Memory is searched.  
The body becomes a room the body cannot leave.

Someone taps through the wall:  
three knocks, silence, two—  
a language made of absence.

Outside, the birds continue their fraudulent music.  
The field keeps shining.

Inside, morning arrives  
wearing yesterday’s bruises.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a postmodern poem titled “This Is Not That Poem,” using unconventional punctuation, enjambment, invented words, repetition, and a closing reference to prisoner number #289-128.
counterfactuals.output:
# This Is Not That Poem

This is not that poem—  
the one with rain behaving  
like rain, politely silvering  
the municipal dark.

No.

This is the poem beside the poem ::  
a margin-creature,  
half footnote / half moth,  
flutterwrit in ungrammar.

It says:

          door door door

until *door* becomes  
a small blue animal  
sleeping under the tongue.

Meanwhile, I—  
(or the typographical rumor of I)—  
misplace the moon  
between two parentheses (

                              )

and call the absence  
moonish.  
Call it unlight.  
Call it neverweather.

This is not that poem.  
This is not that poem.  
This is knot / that poem—

tied to its own undoing,  
enjambed across the stairwell  
where meaning drops  
                         its keys

& every locked metaphor  
dreams itself open.

Reader, you are not reading.  
Writer, I am not written.  
The page is only snow  
performing whiteness  
for an audience of erasers.

Still—

someone scratches a name  
into the sentence-wall;  
someone counts the commas  
as if they were days;

someone whispers  
not freedom, not freedom,  
but the almostword  
freeward—

and the poem ends where it was numbered:

**prisoner #289-128.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw anti-pastoral prison poem in which the speaker apologizes for being unable to turn suffering into comforting art, contrasting peonies, gardenias, and cardinals with screams, blood, suicide, and timeless hell.
counterfactuals.output:
**Apology from the Yard**

Forgive me—I cannot make a meadow of this.

The peonies arrive in their pink abundance  
beyond the razor wire,  
but here a man is screaming  
into the steel mouth of his door  
until his voice becomes blood.

I cannot call that birdsong.

Gardenias open somewhere at dusk,  
white as clean sheets,  
white as the lie of mercy.  
Here, the sheets are knotted  
around a pipe. By morning  
a body hangs in the timeless hell  
between count and count.

Forgive me—I cannot give you beauty  
without its hands cuffed behind it.

A cardinal strikes the fence,  
red sudden against winter,  
and you want it to mean hope.  
But red is already spoken for:  
the floor after the blades,  
the towel pressed uselessly down,  
the thin river leaving a wrist.

I cannot make the blood a rose.  
I cannot make the scream a hymn.  
I cannot turn suicide into a dark tree  
bearing lessons for the living.

The yard has no seasons—  
only heat, cold, concrete, command.  
No shepherd comes. No green field waits.  
The sun itself is searched  
before it enters.

So forgive this poem  
for bringing no gardenia to the grave,  
no peony to soften the cell,  
no cardinal carrying a key in its beak.

I have only the lock,  
the wound,  
the long fluorescent noon  
that never becomes tomorrow.

I have only this:  
hell does not need fire.

It needs a clock  
that does not move.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an intense spoken-word piece from the perspective of a traumatized poet who refuses rhyme and pretty language, calls idealized nature a lie, and questions whether poetry can capture humanity’s evil.
counterfactuals.output:
Do not bring me flowers.

I have seen what grows  
when nobody is watching.

Do not tell me the river is pure.  
The river carries names downstream.  
The river keeps no record.  
The river does not care  
which body was a child.

You call the forest peaceful  
because the trees do not testify.

That is the lie of nature:  
we make it innocent  
because it cannot accuse us.

I have watched sunlight enter a ruined room  
and touch every object equally—  
the broken chair,  
the stain,  
the handprint on the wall.

People call that beautiful.

I call it evidence  
that light has no conscience.

And now you ask me to make a poem.

You want a shape around the damage.  
You want breath measured into lines.  
You want the wound to become something  
you can hold without bleeding.

I refuse.

There is no clean word for what was done.  
There is no image large enough  
to contain a locked door  
and what happened behind it.

Metaphor is a weak witness.

Language arrives after the screaming.  
It takes notes.  
It corrects the grammar.  
It asks whether the horror  
could be made clearer.

Clearer for whom?

Can a poem carry a mass grave  
without turning it into scenery?

Can a sentence look at a human being  
who chose cruelty  
and not invent a reason?

Can words enter the mind of the torturer  
without coming back contaminated?

I do not know.

That is the only honest line I have.

I do not know  
if poetry can hold humanity’s evil.

I know it can point.

I know it can refuse silence.

I know it can stand in the doorway  
with its useless hands open  
and say:

This happened.

A person did this to another person.

No storm made them do it.  
No wolf.  
No winter.  
No darkness.

Do not blame darkness.

Darkness is only the absence of light.

Evil requires a face.  
A decision.  
Someone who could have stopped  
and did not.

Write that down.

Then break the pencil.

It will still not be enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
